utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Please be seated. And may we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we come to the witness of today, some few administrative matters. First of all, as it seems to be usual when one sends out a message, the next day it's already outdated. This is also true for our court schedule until August. As you can see, there was nothing on August the 2nd, but instead of this, there will be a hearing the entire day of 1st August, morning and afternoon. And the 23rd of July, there will be an exchange of courtrooms, and therefore also a change of morning shift and night shift. This means that day, we'll sit instead of the morning, in the afternoon, 23rd of July. The courtroom will be I or III, may I ask the registry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: On the 23rd of July and on the 1st of August, we will move to courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we received a motion by the OTP requesting for subpoena. It is received by the Defence as well? And may I hear some comments to this -- on this issue, please, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you. We did receive just this afternoon the motion seeking a subpoena in connection with this case. We haven't had an opportunity to discuss it with our client at all because we, although we visited him this morning, we didn't receive this until approximately within the last hour. We hope to have a full response for you tomorrow. In essence, we would object to some of it, because we think it's overbroad, namely, paragraph 2 of the proposed subpoena, an order seeking all such original documents, but we would rather reserve our right to explain our position in full tomorrow, if possible, or later this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and let's discuss it a quarter to 7.00 at the end of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we proceed to Witness Number 3. Any changes as regards the protection, the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's just in full open session. Can I just before Your Honour gets to that, ask Your Honours assistance on one matter, and that's the videolink. We would be grateful if Your Honour could give us a date now because there are arrangements that have to be made. We have been given a series of differing dates as to when it is going to take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we indicated that we are open until the 1st of August. All dates are available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We got a message from the registry suggesting some date, and I don't know what the situation is. But we need to know what date they are suggesting, effectively.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be one day during the last week of July, the week of the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which day?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will combine it with other videolinks in another case, so in this case we have to discuss this. If you agree we can do it during this week, then we can arrange the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From our point of view, it's totally open.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Provided, if the registry could be kind of to tell us when the date is suitable for their arrangements, then we can get our arrangements made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will try to do our best together. Any problems from the side of the Defence as regards the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything else? I can't see, so therefore, may the usher please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and give the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. And the examination-in-chief may start.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, is your full name Ivo Atlija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, my full name is Ivo Atlija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 19th of May, 1963, in Brisevo, in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you by ethnic origin a Croat?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you are a Catholic by religion, Roman Catholic by religion?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, just before we deal with the events, I just want to run through with you the various statements you made to the authorities. Whilst you were in Zagreb, in Croatia, did you have an interview with something called the Croatian Information Centre?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after that interview, which took place in January of 1993, was a statement prepared?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, a statement was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And before you signed it, did you take a copy of that statement and discuss it with other refugees from the Brisevo area who had experienced the events?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, when you signed the statement, were you satisfied that it was an accurate reflection and a truthful one of what you had said to the commission?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in October of the year 2000, did you make a statement to investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you given an opportunity to read through the statement that you had made to the Croatian Information Centre?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And make any corrections that you wished to what was in that statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can I come straight away, please, to the area in which you lived until the events of 1992. You were born in the village of Brisevo. Does that come within the local commune of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were there other villages which formed part of that commune, namely, Zune and Raljas?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, please, to look now at a map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that is S14. And I think if we can put it on the ELMO. I think -- could I have it first of all, because I can just get the relevant bit of this map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 14 would be the map of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it would, Your Honour. And it's just easier if I fold the map to the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, if you could look to your left, you will see on the machine next to you, there's a map. And I just want you to indicate -- you have got a pointer there. Could you indicate, first of all -- yes. Can we get more of the map on to -- it may not matter. Whether we can do the focus -- no, to the left, please, as we look at it. Thanks. That's it. Do we see there Ljubija, and then --

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This is Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then going down the map, if we can move the map up slightly, can we see Raljas? I think that's the way to pronounce it. Come down again, sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Can you please just put the map back up a little bit. Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This is the area of Brisevo and Raljas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Thank you very much. That's all I need for the moment although we may need to look at the map later. Was Brisevo a village of approximately 120 houses?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: According to the last 1991 census, yes, about 120 houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that village occupied by Croats, or each house was inhabited by persons of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were only two or three women of Serb ethnicity who were married to Croats from Brisevo. All the others were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there a Catholic church in the village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did most of the men who lived in Brisevo work in the Ljubija iron ore mines?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think they were located within the suburbs of Ljubija itself?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the other villages that you mentioned that came within the Ljubija commune, what was the ethnic makeup of those villages?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Mostly Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about Ljubija town itself?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The town itself, Gornji Ljubija was almost purely Croatian, while Donja Ljubija was predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there a Catholic church in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about elsewhere within the commune?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no Catholic church in Zune.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Raljas?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Raljas was part of the Ljubija parish, and there was a Catholic church in the neighbouring village of Gornja Ravska, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that Ljubija, one part, contained a Muslim population. Were there mosques, therefore, in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a little bit about your background. Did you, in fact, attend high school, it was a technical school, after your elementary education, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in 1982, after you had left school, did you go to do your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which you did for about -- just about 13 months?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you first trained in communications, and then were transferred to the military police.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of your military service, did you become familiar with the uniforms and insignia that were used in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After you had finished your military service, after a couple of months, in 1983, did you get a job at the central repair shop for the Ljubija mines?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you work there until April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that you moved into an apartment in Prijedor town, which had been given to your father, but which you occupied.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after the -- I'm sorry, before the formation of the multinational parties in 1990, were you a member of any political organisation?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of any political organisation or party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After the formation of the national parties, did you join any of them?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you just briefly about the relationships between the different ethnicities in your area, in the Prijedor area generally. Was there any sign of any tensions or anything like that before the election campaign in 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, in my opinion, I would say that we had very good interethnic relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that change, however, as a result of the election campaign?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Even during the election campaign, it began to change.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was it that you most observed as a change?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The greatest change was that people stopped trusting each other and socializing with each other, even at work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what in your view caused that change, that lack of trust?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: In my view, the most important cause was aggressive propaganda by the then recently founded SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say that it was aggressive. What are we talking about? What type of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We're talking about verbal propaganda, first of all, where members of other non-Serb nationalities were publicly called "Ustasha, fundamentalists, balijas, Turks," and other such derogatory names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that this was the SDA propaganda. Were the Croat national party, the HDZ, or the Muslim national party, the SDA, indulging in such propaganda?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They had very few possibilities to reach the media, to use the media, and go public. So that there was no opportunity for them to really counter the SDS with their own propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was it that the SDS had a greater possibility of reaching the media?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Because with the assistance of the JNA, they occupied the repeater at Mrakovica from which -- from then on they started emitting only the Serb programmes and also through the Vjesnik in Prijedor, which were the only local newspapers. And they banned and stopped all other information from Croatia or any other republic where Serbs were not a majority group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly at what date it was, the year, and if possible, the month, that the repeater at Mrakovica was occupied?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think it was in late 1991, or possibly early 1992. I'm not sure, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that the type of propaganda was to use derogatory names such as Ustasha, balijas, Turks, do you recall any other specific propaganda that was relayed?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I will list some of the more drastic examples. Information was released that Dr. Mirza Mujadzic had given pregnant Serb women injections, the consequences of which that those women could only give birth to female children and the birth rate among Serbs in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina was thus reduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where did you hear that, with a that on television or the radio or did you hear that at some kind of a meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That was on Radio Prijedor, and then it spread by the word of mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Serbs, for example, that you worked with to this propaganda? Did they accept it, or were they skeptical?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: In my view, the reaction was difficult to understand, because they accepted this propaganda without giving it a second thought or question if anything like that was possible. As far as I know about medicine, there is no way to tell the gender of a child, to determine the gender of a child in advance, especially not by injection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this sort of type of propaganda, what effect was it having on the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We lived in great fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you notice an increase in the carrying of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: In the town of Prijedor itself, there was an enormous amount of armed persons in the streets, in the cafes, all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those armed persons, were those members of the military, the regular JNA? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They wore the uniforms and insignia of the then regular JNA, but there were armed people in the -- wearing police uniforms, the police that was then referred to as "Milicija".

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The increase in armed persons, was that true of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Mostly armed people walking around were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you speak to any of the Serbs that you knew about why they were carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what explanation did you get?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The most frequent explanation was that they only wanted to successfully defend Yugoslavia and for all Serbs to live within one state, and that they would never allow that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to become Croatian, Ustasha soil, or a dzemaharija, which was a derogatory name they used for a state in which Muslims would live and be in power, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give us again a rough idea of when you first noticed the increase in armed men in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Most frequently, end of March, beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come now, then, to the events at the end of April. You told us earlier that your last day of work at the repair shop was April 1992. How did it come about that your work there ceased?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I went to work in the morning, and I saw checkpoints, bunkers, along the road, armed Serb soldiers, Serb flags outside the municipality building. I came to my work, and the manager told us that orders had arrived that the SDS had taken power in Prijedor, and that we should now disperse and go back to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us you saw checkpoints, bunkers, and then armed Serb soldiers. Again, were those members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They wore uniforms of the former JNA, but there were policemen, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any persons manning these checkpoints or bunkers who were not wearing uniforms of the former JNA but a different sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, but fewer. Some wore only parts of the uniform and were not wearing the five-pointed star, the insignia of the JNA, but a cross with four S's, instead, or the so called Kokardas from the Second World War that the Chetniks used to wear in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were told that orders had arrived by the manager -- sorry, start that again. The manager told you that the SDS had taken power in Prijedor, and that you should disperse and go back to your homes. Did you return to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I did not return to my own flat, but I look the bus to Ljubija, and there on, I walked to my native village of Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you thereafter, for the next few months, remain in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it possible to travel to Prijedor from Brisevo without any difficulty during that period?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: You needed to have a permit from the Serb authorities in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you during that period go back to Prijedor at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to the apartment that you had been occupying in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One of my colleagues from work, a lady who had remained in Prijedor, let me know through her brother in Ljubija who walked to my place in Ljubija that a Serb, Milan Mutic, from Donja Ljubija, had moved into my apartment and he was still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you make any attempts through the authorities to have him removed?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't try anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Simply, I was scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move next, please, to what happened in May of 1992. From your location in Brisevo, were you able to see villages which were predominantly Muslim ones, such as Kozarac, Hambarine, Carakovo, Rizvanovici, Biscani, Zecovi, and Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One could see that very well because Brisevo is on a higher altitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In May of 1992, did you have coming to Brisevo people seeking refuge?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: May 1992, there was a large group of people coming from the village of Hambarine, and we kept them in our homes for about seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that before or after the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This was the day of the attack on Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you personally heard or saw of that attack.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, personally, I was able to see only people who were quite small, because I was at a distance. I saw a number of tanks firing at Hambarine. I could hear the shooting very clearly and seeing people move in the direction of Hambarine, soldiers stopping and moving towards Hambarine. I could see houses burning. I could see smoke and hear detonations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the attack took place, did you hear anything being said on the radio in respect of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Before the attack, Radio Prijedor, for a number of hours, broadcast the so-called ultimatum for a person called Aziz Aliskovic to surrender. If he did not do so, Hambarine would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you know who this person was, or why he was being ordered to surrender?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I knew that he used to be a policeman, and I knew that a small group of Serb young men was shooting at Hambarine, at a checkpoint or at a house, and that Aziz Aliskovic, if that was his name, tried to resist. And that was the reason, or should have been the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you could see a number of tanks that were involved in the attack, and you could see people move in the direction of Hambarine, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can you remember roughly how many tanks you saw?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, two or three tanks. There were not very many. There was not a large of number of tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The soldiers, roughly, could you tell how many there were taking part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is difficult to say, but I think there may have been about a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from your viewpoint, were you able to see whether this was the regular JNA or what you've described as people who were not in proper military uniform, or full military uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't really distinguish between these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say you saw the tanks firing. How long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It didn't last a long time, a few hours only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody firing back from the village, any returning fire from mortars or other artillery?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see, but I could hear individual shots from Hambarine to the Prijedor Polje from where the Serb soldiers were coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once the tanks had stopped firing, what did the soldiers do that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I saw when the soldiers were moving forward and when the shots were coming from Hambarine. They would lie down. I didn't see whether they were wounded or anything, but then the group would move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you've told us, I think, that you saw houses on fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, was the -- were -- the fires to the houses, were they caused by people, the infantry going into the village, or by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't see whether they were torching or whether it was due to the artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us that that same day, a number of refugees arrived from the area. What kind of refugees? In other words, men, women, children, a mixture?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were mostly women, children, elderly men, and there were some younger men but not so many.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And roughly how many were there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Perhaps about 400.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of these refugees about what they had experienced?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What generally did they tell you had happened to them and their families?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They were terrified, and they kept saying that the Serbs were killing everyone they could see, that they were raping women, and torching houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any of the women tell you that they personally had been raped?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I didn't ask, nor did any of the women tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was Hambarine. Did you see any other villages being attacked during the following days?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One could see the attack on Kozarac very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you see happening in the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, the distance from us to Kozarac is a little larger, so we could only hear the detonations, the explosions. We could see houses burning, and this went on for days. I think seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any refugees from the Kozarac area as a result -- who came to your village as a result?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I don't know of anyone from Kozarac coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Carakovo and Rizvanovici? Did you see anything happening to those villages?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We couldn't see those villages in detail, but we could hear the detonations. We could see the fire and the smoke. But from those villages, refugees did come to Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whilst these villages were being attacked, did you hear announcements or what Prijedor Radio was broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: This was, again, a typical propaganda. They boasted of great successes of the Serb army, and they kept saying that an Ustasha fundamentalist stronghold had fallen, and that a large number of Ustashas and Green Berets had been liquidated and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When these announcements were being made, did the radio say on whose behalf those announcements were making, who was making those announcements?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It was most frequently said that "on the behalf of the Crisis Staff," of the so-called Crisis Staff that was operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I move then, please to the 27th of May of 1992. Did something wake you that morning?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think it was May -- on 27th of May, there was an explosion of mortar shells that woke me up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was that explosion?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Near the home where I was sleeping, near my home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So -- sorry. It was in your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it -- one explosion woke you up. Were there further explosions after that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling continued, in a continued fashion actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you see where the shelling was coming from?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They were coming from the village of Rasavci and Ostra Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have a look again at the map, I'm not sure the villages are shown on the map, but if we just have another look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, yes, if you would indicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, bring it up to...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are Rasavci, Rasavci are here. And here is Ostra Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, could you just indicate that again. Would you be so kind.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Rasavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: And to the south, Ostra Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Thank you. We can see it written across the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it written across the map. That's what was confusing me slightly. All right, so that was the area from which the shelling was coming. Could you see where the shells, what type of shells there were? In other words, were they tanks or mortars or other weaponry, or field guns?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were only mortar shells on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And those two places that you've mentioned, what ethnicity were the inhabitants of those villages or areas?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Those were Serb villages with a hundred per cent Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you able to see this because you and some other men from your village went to have a look?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is right. We went to a point where we could see Rasavci and Ostra Luka both.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How much damage did the shelling do to the village that first day?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: On the first day, there was practically no damage, no physical damage, no one was wounded on that first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before that shelling started, had there been any kind of warning or ultimatum which had been given to your village of Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Having seen where this was coming from, did you join the other men of the village in the village hall?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did you all decide to do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We decided to send a delegation to Rasavci and Ostra Luka to ask why we were being attacked, because we were not guilty of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who -- how many men made up that delegation?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Five or six men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did they go to the village, or to the area, Ostra Luka?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When they came back, what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They told us that the Serbs had issued an ultimatum that we had to surrender all our weapons, including the Bofors, and if they didn't, they would search the houses. And if they were to find the weapons there, the houses would be burnt down, and the owner of the house arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we come to the question of weapons in your village. How many people had weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, five or six hunting rifles, and a few pistols which the people owned and had legal permits for that. But Bofors and other types of weapons of that kind did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that twice, the Bofors gun, was that something the Serbs had mentioned to your delegation?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They claimed that they had seen those guns in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us you didn't have them. Just for the purposes, if you know what they are, can you describe to the Court, who may be more conversant with weaponry than me, but what is a Bofors gun?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It is an anti-aircraft weapon. I don't know its calibre. It has a semi-automatic firing. It is mounted on vehicles. Usually, there are two or three barrels turned towards the sky. I don't know how to explain this, describe this better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had your village ever -- the TO in your village, had they ever possessed a weapon like that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No. I never seen weapons of this kind anywhere in the village, nor with the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What had happened to the weaponry that the TO had had?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It had been returned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So they were saying that they wanted the surrender of all your weapons with the accompanying threat. What did you -- the villagers decide to do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We picked up our hunting guns and some of the pistols, I don't know the exact number, and we handed them over to those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, we didn't want to provoke them additionally, and we knew that no one had any possibility to defend oneself with weapons of that kind against the army and people who were better armed than us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That day, before the decision was taken to surrender the weapons, had there been anybody firing in response -- I'm sorry, firing from your village in response to the shelling that was going on?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Not a single bullet was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So, you handed over the weapons. Was that taken to Rasavci by another delegation?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Another delegation of people took the weapons to Rasavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when they returned, what did they tell you had happened after the surrender of the weapons? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They said that the representatives of the Serbs, of the Serb army were very angry because they demanded much more weapons and the famous Bofors they wanted as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did they say they would do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They said that they would send a delegation that would, together with some people, some inhabitants of our village, search their houses, and then the threats were the same, that the owner of the house would be killed and the house set on fire. And our delegation said that they agreed, and that they could come and look for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any search take place that day or in the following day?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, there were no searches ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you receive any visits from any of the authorities in order to conduct a search?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, no one ever visited us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that was the 27th, 28th of May. Did anything happen in the next few weeks?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, it was peaceful. And then there were some incidents. In the first few weeks, it was comparatively peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you, the villagers, able to leave the village to go and buy food supplies?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The village was totally blocked. No one could come in; no one could go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what blocked it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, all around in the woods and along the roads, everywhere Serb soldiers were positioned. Whether they were manning checkpoints or in ditches or walking around freely, they were there, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, can I ask you, what type of soldiers are we talking about? Regular JNA or irregular?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, most of them were wearing JNA uniforms and insignia, but there were others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did anybody try and pass those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Dimac Radislav tried to pass a checkpoint in the neighbouring village, in Gornja Ravska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Where the road separates for Gornja Ravska several soldiers caught him and beat him up, and he was returned, along with some children, to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us that you couldn't leave. How did you survive?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Most of the inhabitants of Brisevo had their gardens, their vegetable plots, and there was some amounts of food. So for some time, we could live comparatively normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The situation was critical for the two people who had diabetes because we couldn't get any insulin. And the rest, we somehow managed to get.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did there come a time on the 24th of June when some arrests were made?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, who effected the arrests? Who came to make those arrests?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: A police van from Ljubija drove up, and three or four police officers arrived outside the shop in Brisevo and made several arrests there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the policemen?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult for me to remember now, but I have named these people in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: For example, I think Dragan Vukic from Ljubija was one of them. Bijekic, Baja Bijekic, as they called him, was also among of them. But there were not only two of them, there were more people. Rade Zekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these policemen?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I think they were Serbs. Concerning Mr. Bijekic, I think he was even a Croat. I'm not quite sure, but I think he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The men who were arrested, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Outside the shop, I think they arrested two citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you present at the arrests?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I was standing at around 15 or 20 metres from the scene, at most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was any reason given that you heard for these arrests?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They didn't call it an "arrest." They said they were taking those people for an interview, for a brief interview, in the police station in Ljubija, an information interview, as they used to refer to it in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So those, you think there were two men then. Anybody else either taken or go to the police station in Ljubija at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That same day, they continued with the van to Jozo Buzuk's house and Juro Jakara's house. Some people, they weren't home, and they left a note for them to report to the police station in Ljubija the next day for other such interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did the men go?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Two of them didn't. I didn't go, and Emil Kovidovic didn't go. The rest of them did go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And roughly in all, was that who went?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Vinko Mlinar went. His father, Slavko Mlinar, went, too. Juro Marijan went, and another man whose name I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there were two taken off, and another four people after that. What happened to those six people? Did they return to the village that night or later?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They never returned at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those men?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We later found out at first they were questioned and beaten in Ljubija, and then they were taken to the Keraterm camp, then to Omarska, and from Omarska to Manjaca. From Manjaca, then to Bijeljina, and from Bijeljina to some small village, and later on they were exchanged. Some, however, were killed and never returned. They were killed in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there anything about these men that provided a link as to why they should have been taken or asked to go to the police station for interview?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I can't find any such link or inherent logic except that Vinko and Slavko Mlinar were son and father. And perhaps because they took off one of them they also took the other. But apart from that, I can't really find a real reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any of these men heavily involved in political life, for example?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, not one of them was actively involved in politics. Whether any one of them was a member of some party, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were any of them leaders within the -- your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We were not really organised in such a way as to have a leader or anything like that. There was no leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that was in June. Were there any other incidents that took place before the attack started on your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were two other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the first?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I can't remember the date exactly, but it was in late June. In Ljubija, Dragan Dizdarevic was arrested outside in the street and was taken to a camp. In mid-July, Milan Ivandic was beaten and cut with a screwdriver.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That was just below his house, perhaps a hundred fifty metres from his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's actually the borderline between Brisevo and Rasavci. There's a field there and a forest, so it's difficult to draw the line between the two villages with any precision. We never knew the exact boundary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who beat him and cut him with a screwdriver?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: A number of young Serb men from Rasavci came over. They called Milan and his brothers to help them pull a car out of the bog. When they came, they first offered them brandy and made them sing with them. And after that, they maltreated them, beat them, and poked them, cut them up with screwdrivers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come, then, to the day before the attack. That day, did you decide to go swimming?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where were you going to swim?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We went to a lake in the neighbouring village of Stara Rijeka. In order to get to it, you had to pass through Stara Kipe. Kipe were remnants of iron ores. When you blow up a hill, then the hole fills up with water, and that's how the lake was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On your way to the lake, did you pass any checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There weren't any checkpoints around the lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whilst you were there, did a cousin of yours arrive, Branko Atlija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: He was all in panic, and he said that Zoran Marjanovic from Ostra Luka, a Serb, had come to his place and told us to run because Brisevo, Brisevo would be cleansed the next day. That two brigades were preparing to cleanse Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say this was a Serb. Did he explain why he had come to give this warning, or did your cousin know why he had given this warning?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Because his sister was married to a Croat, and he had tried to convince his sister and her husband to hide in his house in Ostra Luka because he thought they would be safe there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When your cousin gave you this information, did you believe this?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No one believed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We just dispersed, went home. We didn't really have a choice. If they should attack us, we thought we would run in smaller groups because that way we would have better chances of survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did the attack actually start?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Half past 3.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that the following, the early hours of the following morning, the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of that attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I was woken up again by explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were the explosions the same type as had earlier happened in -- when you were shelled in May?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were all possible explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean there were different kinds of explosions?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. There were many kinds of explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of the explosions, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: My parents decided to hide in a neighbour's cellar that that could be used as some sort of shelter, and I ran to the adjacent house owned by Marko Buzuk, so we tried to arrange something to see what we could do in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you left your house, what was happening? Was there any damage at that stage?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't see any damage at that point, but there were explosions very near. And between the explosions, there were very short intervals. I had to lie down all the time as I ran.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got to your neighbour's -- I'm sorry, to the house of Marko Buzuk, were there other people already there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were other people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where were the people congregated?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They were all in the cellar under the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you, then, decide together with Milan Buzuk to go to another house?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Together with his son, Milan Buzuk, I decided to go to another house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We wanted to see how many people there were in the other house, and to see whether they had any idea and whether we could do something together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And to whose did you then go?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The owner of that house was Luka Mlinar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, were there a number of people at his house?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were a number of people there, but fewer than in the first house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So how did the events progress during the early hours of that morning?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As time went by, infantry fire increased, not only artillery but also infantry fire, from infantry automatic weapons. We also had the first casualties, the first -- some people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long did the artillery and the infantry fire continue for?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: For the whole day. The following night, it abated slightly, but it did not cease all together. And then it resumed again the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see, during that first day, what damage was being caused, or did you remain in the basement of a house?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't see much really. In the afternoon, I came out of the cellar of that house, and we went back to the cellar of Marko Buzuk's house. And then I left that cellar, too, and I fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I ran to a place where my parents and several neighbours were sheltered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that in a house?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That was in the cellar of a house owned by Pero Dimac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And sir, you say that the shelling continued all day, abated slightly in the evening, but then started again the following morning.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that morning, did the Serb infantry arrive?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The Serb infantry entered the village in the evening, but I couldn't see them from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm about to come on to the next part. I don't know whether that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The trial stays adjourned until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Thank you. May you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, we had just reached the point when you told us that the infantry arrived in the village in the evening. When they arrived, whereabouts were you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I was still in the cellar where my parents where. The house and the cellar were in a valley in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you learn, then, of the arrival of the infantry?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We could hear strong infantry fire, bullets were flying all over. And we could hear them yelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the first sighting that you had of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The morning of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did you first see them?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At about 200 metres from the cellar where I was hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there a window in the cellar so that you could see out?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There were two windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The soldiers that you saw as you looked out, were they in regular JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They were wearing JNA uniforms with red ribbons around their arms, and some tied those red ribbons around their helmets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were in the basement. Did any soldiers come there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: A group of some 10 or 12 soldiers came just outside the cellar, but they did not go in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who opened the door?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: My father and Pero Dimac went outside to face them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did the soldiers say or do to your father and Mr. Dimac?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At first, they only yelled, and they said: "Why are you firing at us? Why are you firing at the Serb army? Hand over your weapons." They were saying something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what response did they get from your father or Mr. Dimac?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: My father said: "We're not shooting, and we have no weapons. The only one's shooting around here is you."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How many of you were in the basement at that stage when the soldiers arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: My father, Pero Dimac, my mother, Franjo Dimac, Janje [phoen] Dimac, myself, and Viktor Tozan. Seven persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your father having told them that nobody was shooting, what did the soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They talked in a normal tone of voice. They said we should disperse and go each to their homes, that no one would do anything to us, that their task was completed. And then they continued on towards the Catholic church in Brisevo alongside a hill. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so did you all disperse?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We did disperse, but we did not all go to our respective homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Together with two friends, I went to the adjacent house to see what had happened to them, whether they were still alive or whether they had been taken off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The owner of the house was Ivica Dimac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived there, that is, the house of Ivica Dimac, did anything happen, or did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: After about 10 minutes, we heard shouts from Pero Dimac's house, Pero Dimac's house, which is about 140 metres far from the other house. So we could hear the shouts very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Pero Dimac still with you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: He left his house, came out of the basement, and stayed in front of his own house when we left. And my father and mother left and went towards our own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you heard the shouts coming from Pero Dimac's house. What did you see happening and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We ran towards Pero Dimac's house, and we saw two soldiers wearing JNA uniforms but on their heads they had Subara hats with Kokardas, they were unshaven with long beards, and they were engaged in a fervent discussion with my mother and Pero Dimac, and then they left and joined the other soldiers who were headed for the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that they were wearing JNA uniforms, but on their heads they had Subara hats, what did that suggest to you? In other words, were they regular JNA soldiers or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I can't really say now. But it was quite usual for soldiers with such insignia, where we come from, to be called "the Chetniks." That's from World War II. Those were paramilitary units in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there anything else that distinguished what came to be called the Chetnik soldiers from regular JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Regular JNA soldiers, for example, one detail, the knife they usually wore was part of the automatic rifle K-47 kit, A-47 or AB or AB 2, depending on the type of rifle they were using. And these soldiers wore a very different kind of knives, hunting knives, knives used for civilian purposes. They are not really part of any military kit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there had been something happening between your mother and Pero and these soldiers. They went towards the church. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We ran to Pero's and to my mother's, and the two soldiers didn't notice us. They didn't want to notice us. They didn't react to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of state were your mother and Pero in?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Pero was pale, and my mother was crying and shouting. She said: "Run away, run off, they killed your father. Go wherever you can."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: We ran across a brook, and we crouched behind a small tree in a small woods. And Pero and my mother remained in front of the house. They couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to Pero and your mother?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: After a few moments, a large group of soldiers, several hundreds of people came, and they locked up my mother in the pigsty, and Pero was thrown off onto the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there still firing going on at that stage, shooting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, there was -- the shooting hadn't stopped at any single moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there was still artillery firing going on, was there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The explosions echoed, but they were in front of the -- a few metres in front of the infantry lines, in front of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that your mother was locked up in the pigsty, and Pero was thrown off onto the road. What did you see happen to Pero?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Three or four soldiers beat Pero. They swore at him. They found the Bible in his house, and they said: "Let the Catholic Jesus help him now." They swore at his mother and asked why Tudjman wasn't helping him then. They made him take off his clothes, and he was in his underwear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that they found a Bible in his house. What did they do with the Bible?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: First, they hit Pero with it, and then they threw it back into the house, and then they set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that they made Pero take off his clothes. First, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, at the time, he must have been 65, 66. Not more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after they had made him strip, what sort of position was he in? Was he standing, lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: No, he was not lying on the ground. He was being beaten, and then he was falling from one side to another after having beaten. And then he would fall down, and then they made him run from one to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before they had hit him, as you told us, with the Bible, and before they threw it back in the house, did they make him do anything else with the Bible?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They made him to pray according to the Catholic ritual, and then made fun of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So having beaten him, you say they made him run from one to the other. How did the whole incident come to an end?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One of the soldiers ordered him to run in the direction of where we were hiding, Viktor Tozan and I, and then he shot him in the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During this, did Pero offer any resistance at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Pero was crying, and I didn't see that he even tried to defend himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After he had been shot, did any of the soldiers say anything that you heard?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, two soldiers approached him. They asked: "Where is he"? And the other one said: "The Ustasha dog fell into the water."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think that you drew a sketch plan of what you saw and where you were when this happened. I wonder if it could be shown, please, the document that was Annex D to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I believe Your Honours have copies of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, perhaps if you can just indicate - I think - do we see on the far left-hand side you've indicated where you were? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Where I was is marked by a cross, and the I. A. Initials stand there, and V. T., Viktor Tozan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where we see the initials P. D., is that where Dimac was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that was the place where Pero Dimac was killed. And the little square represents his house, the location of his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And have you indicated the locations of other houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I marked the location of houses that were the closest to the scene of that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, we see there were a number of other Dimac houses to, as we look at it, the right of where Pero was killed.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you indicating, by the line that we can see through there, the road?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the village road. It's not asphalt. It's an ordinary road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, if we go to the top right-hand corner, have you marked there what we can see as the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. That is where the Catholic church was, but I would like to point out that the scale is perhaps not very good, and perhaps the distance is not correctly represented, the distance between the church and the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. And does the road divide there? Is that what you're indicating?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It divides into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that it goes in one direction to Marijani and the other to Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, unless there's an objection, may that be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Entered into evidence as S183. S183.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after that, what did you see was happening in your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: For a few hours, we remained concealed in that same place, and we saw that houses were burning around that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What were the soldiers doing?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The soldiers were passing by. For a long time, there was a big group passing, and then smaller groups were passing. And then individual soldiers were passing. Some of them were driving things that had been looted. Some simply passed by. Others were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, again, the soldiers, were they JNA, Chetniks, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: There was a mixture. But I would like to point out that most of them had regular insignia on them, the JNA insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that some of them were driving things that had been looted. What sort of things were they looting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Mainly technical goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by that do you mean -- I'm sorry, what do you mean by "technical goods"?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Television sets, air-conditioning sets, videos, hi-fis, and some pieces of furniture, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how were they driving them off? Were they driving trucks, army trucks, or were they taking people's vehicles?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I saw civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were those vehicles that belonged to your village or people who lived in your village, or did they come in from outside?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, only two tractors were from our village, taken from our village. But the origin of the other vehicles, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you saw that houses were burning. How were they being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Well, the fire appeared from inside. I don't know how the fires were set, but the fire always appeared from the inside. And when it reached a certain level, it would reach the roof, and the roof would cave in, and the flames would come outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there officers present?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I was able to see only three or four people with officers' insignia, those who were nearer to our hiding point. The others, I couldn't see whether they held ranks or whether they were ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any of the officers, either the ones who were near you or that you could see further off, make any attempt to prevent the looting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I didn't notice that anyone tried to prevent the looting or the beating or killing of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say there were three or four officers who were near to your hiding point. Did you hear them speak?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: One of the soldiers had a radio station on his back, and he was shouting quite loudly because there was something wrong with the links. They said: "9th Battalion deploy, go more forward," and things to that effect. In any case, they were making a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These officers, were you able to tell where they came from?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't conclude from where they were -- where they came from. They spoke the Ekavian dialect. But the Ekavian language is the official language of the army, so they were not necessarily from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say you heard the -- one of the officers shouting into a radio and giving orders, for example, to the 9th Battalion. Did you hear any arrangements being made as to where they would meet? Where the units would meet?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: They were all being asked to go in the direction of the Catholic church and to meet at the point called Dizdari, it is a hill not too far from the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that stage, did you know which units, which brigade of the JNA was engaged in this attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: At that time, this area was held by the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know where that brigade was based?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: You're referring to the headquarters where the command of the brigade was or where the barracks were?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The command.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: The command of the 6th Krajina Brigade, well, I cannot tell you exactly where the command was. But the operational command, which was carrying out this operation, it was located in Dizdari hill in the house of Phillip Dizdari. That's where the command was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how were you able to find that out?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: An inhabitant, Vlado Dimac, told me that. He was caught and taken to the command. And there at the command, this Major Veljko Brajic said that. And he said that he was in charge of the operation, and this was his command, and he spoke with Vlado Dimac the whole evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any other units in the area, or brigades that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. In the direction of Prijedor and Ljubija, there was the 5th Kozara Brigade. I think that it changed its name later on, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you able to establish which units did take part, which brigades did take part in this attack, at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Subsequently, I found out from other victims of that event that from the side of Sanski Most, that there was the 6th Krajina Brigade, and towards the north, it was the 5th Kozara Brigade, and then they joined, and they created a ring, and they got together. They joined at Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In a moment, I'm going to ask you to look at another drawing that you did to assist Court on the attack, but you heard from other victims. Did you receive any kind of official confirmation from anybody in a position to know that either of the two units had taken part, the two brigades, I should say?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Later on, Mr. Vojo Kupresanin confirmed this, but he said it was only a minor incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at and explain to us the map you drew to explain the attack, which was attached as Annex E to your statement. Now, I think the best thing would be, Mr. Atlija, if you could explain to us what you're indicating on this particular drawing.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
utterances.text: Okay. Here you can see the northern direction, from the direction of Ljubija. And on this -- from this side, the members of the 5th Kozara Brigade were coming. And behind the direction of their action, I wrote down which territorial units were part of that brigade then, the reserve, the Territorial Defence of Ljubija, Ljeskare and Miska Glava and so on. And from the south, from the direction of Sanski Most, through the Stara Rijeka, Ostra Luka, and Rasavci villages, the members of the 6th Krajina Brigade came. I said that the 5th, 6th, and 8th Battalion that took part in this because I heard orders of the commanders with regard to that battalion. For the others, I could not really find out whether all the battalions of the brigade had taken part or only some. The arrows show the direction in which the infantry encircled the village, and on the second day of the attack, they descended into the valley in the very centre of the village, and they gathered here on the Dizdari hill which has been indicated by a larger dot. And then from there, they dispersed once the action had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you -- I think in fact, the map itself was drawn by yourself and another survivor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA
